analysis.one_liner: Lets states run coal ash disposal permit programs instead of the EPA, blocking stricter federal rules.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 267-144 on October 14, 2011, but the Senate never voted, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Coal-burning power plants produce millions of tons of coal ash, which sits in ponds and landfills that can leak into groundwater or fail catastrophically, as one did in Tennessee in 2008. This bill would have set up a state-by-state permitting system for coal ash disposal, with the EPA stepping in only when a state refused or failed. It would also have barred the EPA from ever regulating coal ash as hazardous waste. The House passed it along mostly party lines; the Senate never brought it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal-burning electric utilities, which avoid the cost of treating and disposing of coal ash under stricter federal hazardous-waste rules, and coal producers, whose product's disposal footprint stays cheaper to manage.

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes states to adopt coal combustion residuals permit programs, with the EPA required to step in only if a governor opts out, the state fails to certify a program, or the state fails to fix deficiencies the EPA identifies.

Sets minimum criteria for state programs: structures must contain maximum ash volumes, new units must be built two feet above the water table, and programs must include groundwater monitoring, corrective action, location restrictions, financial assurance, and closure rules.
Requires that surface impoundment closure plans at minimum remove liquid and stabilize remaining waste.
Excludes coal ash used or stored at surface mining and reclamation operations from any EPA-run program.

analysis.who_pays: People living near coal ash ponds and landfills, who would bear the risk of groundwater contamination and spills under a patchwork of state programs that can each waive requirements it judges unneeded, and taxpayers who could foot cleanup bills when impoundments fail.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near coal ash disposal sites

drawbacks.text: A state may decline to apply any of the bill's criteria it determines is not needed for managing coal ash in that state; the EPA can treat that as a deficiency, but the state gets notice and an opportunity to remedy it, and control shifts back once fixed.

The bill prohibits any construction that would alter EPA's 2000 determination that fossil fuel combustion wastes do not warrant regulation as hazardous waste, foreclosing the stricter federal option entirely.
The bill's requirements apply only through state permit programs; in states that decline to run one, the EPA implements a program, but states otherwise retain control and the EPA must defer to them.

Supporters' honest case: the bill would have created the first enforceable federal minimum standards for coal ash — containment, groundwater monitoring, financial assurance, closure — replacing non-binding federal guidance, while keeping decisions close to state regulators who know their sites.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's minimum criteria were real and would have been an improvement over no enforceable standards at all, but its core effect was to preempt a stricter federal rule then in development at the EPA and to let individual states waive requirements. For a waste stream that has contaminated drinking water and produced billion-dollar dam failures, the trade — industry convenience in exchange for uneven, waivable state protection — favored the industry disposing of the ash.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 267-144 in October 2011, but the Senate never brought it to a vote, and it expired when that Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: The House Energy and Commerce Committee reported the bill amended on September 26, 2011, and the Rules Committee granted it one hour of debate with a closed amendment process allowing only specified amendments.
Amendments offered by Reps. Waxman, Markey, and Rush were each rejected after debate under the rule.

A motion to recommit with instructions to add a public warning system for potential catastrophic failures at coal ash disposal sites failed 172-238, with all 172 supporting votes coming from Democrats.
Final passage passed 267-144: 230 of 241 Republicans in favor, while Democrats opposed it 141-37.
The Senate received the bill and placed it on its calendar on October 17-18, 2011, but no further action was taken before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Communities near coal ash disposal sites and the EPA came out ahead: by dying in the Senate, the bill left the EPA free to later write federal coal ash disposal rules of its own instead of being locked into the state-by-state system this bill prescribed.

sides.party_line_note: Republicans backed it nearly unanimously (230-3) while Democrats opposed it nearly as lopsidedly (141-37), making the House vote a mostly party-line split.

industries.note: The bill would have replaced EPA's pending federal coal ash rules with state permit programs whose requirements states could individually waive, sparing utilities the cost of hazardous-waste handling. The cost — leak and failure risk at ash ponds and landfills — falls on the communities living around them.
The bill exempts the use, placement, and storage of coal ash at surface mining and reclamation operations from any EPA-run program, keeping a major disposal outlet unregulated at the federal level.

industries.industry: Coal ash recycling and disposal services
industries.note: The bill is framed to facilitate recovery and beneficial use of coal residuals and locks in state-permitted land-based disposal as the permanent management channel, rather than a federal hazardous-waste regime that could have pushed toward elimination or stricter containment.
